A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Top-k and adaptive Top-k(x) Learning-to-Defer work. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite v4's expanded scope and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original California Housing regression and SVHN/CIFAR-100 classification experiments in Section 5 and Appendices A.13–A.14, including performance curves and expert scores.

after.justification: v4 retains original two-stage experiments and adds one-stage CIFAR-10 and SVHN evaluations in Appendix B.2, including new expert scores and performance curves.

M1.justification: v1 proposes multi-expert selection for two-stage L2D with a fixed base predictor. v4 adds a one-stage procedure that jointly scores class-label and expert entities through an augmented classifier. The existing two-stage surrogate and subsequent cardinality training remain; the substantive change is this additional learning regime.

E1.justification: v4 adds CIFAR-10 classification in Appendix B.2.1 while retaining CIFAR-100, SVHN, and California Housing. This extends coverage within the existing image-classification domain; the one-stage training configurations are protocol changes rather than additional datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: v4 Figures 5–6 add a one-stage Top-1 comparator attributed to Mozannar and Sontag (2020) and Mao et al. (2024a). California's random/oracle comparison in v1 Figure 5(a) disappears: v4 Figure 7(a) duplicates 7(b), despite retaining the baseline caption. Additional citations attached to retained two-stage Top-1 points do not establish separately evaluated methods.

E3.justification: Appendix B.2 introduces distinct one-stage evaluation protocols with six experts and joint class/expert scoring. These include a ResNet-4 policy trained for 200 epochs and SVHN specialist ResNet-18 experts trained for 20 epochs on class-specific subsets. The existing two-stage experiments retain their stated splits, metrics, architectures, and training budgets.

E4.justification: v4 extends cardinality and aggregation sensitivity analyses to one-stage selection. Figures 5(c–d) and 6(c–d) examine how voting accuracy changes as more entities are selected, including deterioration at larger cardinalities. The corresponding two-stage analyses were already present in v1 and remain.

E5.justification: v1 Appendix A.13.4 and v4 Section 8 both specify four independent runs with fixed experts, fifty repetitions for random policies, and one-standard-deviation error bars. Although v4 changes the wording from mean and variance to mean and standard deviation, the documented plotting practice and retained uncertainty displays are unchanged.

E6.justification: v4 adds one-stage expert scores and performance curves for CIFAR-10 and SVHN. For example, Appendix B.2.1 reports CIFAR-10 majority-voting accuracy of 95.53% at budget 0.192 for Top-k(x), versus a fixed-k best of 94.7% at 0.199. These are new results, not improvements over v1 under matched conditions. Existing two-stage score tables remain unchanged, but California's random/oracle curves are lost.

T1.justification: v4 adds formal one-stage entity-cost definitions, a unified one-/two-stage consistency theorem with explicit kS scaling, and proofs recovering special cases including selective prediction. It also revises the cascade separation argument. Conversely, v1's optimal-cardinality Lemma 4.8 and its Appendix A.11 proof are removed rather than relocated.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the contribution from a generalization of two-stage L2D to a unified framework covering one-stage and two-stage L2D, selective prediction, and cascades. v4 adds an explicit one-stage Hh-consistency claim while retaining the central adaptive-cardinality and accuracy–cost claims.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations of why one-stage selection requires costs accounting for both labels and experts, and interprets the consistency bound's explicit dependence on k. It drops v1 Appendix A.4.3's assertion that all consistency guarantees automatically extend to classical cascades. Existing interpretations concerning over-querying, weighted aggregation, and cost-aware selection largely remain.

D1.justification: v4 documents expert construction and training configurations for the new one-stage experiments and explicitly specifies tie-breaking rules. It retains the A100 hardware disclosure and existing two-stage configurations, but removes v1's per-dataset GPU memory measurements and explicit choice of the linear penalty function xi(v)=v.

R1.justification: Section 2 expands from positioning the work between two-stage L2D and top-k classification to addressing both L2D regimes. It adds substantial one-stage calibration, surrogate, and human–AI collaboration literature, including Cao et al., Charusaie et al., and additional Mao et al. works, and broadens the claimed research gap accordingly.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, preliminaries, and method exposition are extensively rewritten around unified policy and entity terminology. Adaptive cardinality moves from Section 4.4 to a standalone Section 5, experiments receive a separate Appendix B, and reproducibility becomes a main-text section. These changes substantially reorganize the narrative.

P2.justification: v4 substantially reformats typography, author information, running headers, and figure/table placement. It adds two multi-panel experimental figures and two expert-score tables, and updates the inference diagrams. Retained two-stage plots are largely redisplayed unchanged, but Figure 7(a) erroneously duplicates 7(b), replacing the earlier California baseline panel.

improvement.justification: The implemented one-stage extension, accompanying analysis, and CIFAR-10/SVHN evaluations broaden supported applicability, while the revised cascade argument improves exposition. These gains are tempered by removal of the explicit optimal-cardinality lemma and proof despite retaining the optimal-cardinality claim, and by Figure 7(a)'s duplication, which removes California baseline evidence. Together, these support a limited net quality improvement.
